title: Color Fault-Tolerant Spanners
classifications: Theory of computation → Sparsification and spanners
abstract:
We initiate the study of spanners in arbitrarily vertex- or edge-colored graphs (with no "legality" restrictions), that are resilient to failures of entire color classes. When a color fails, all vertices/edges of that color crash. An f-color fault-tolerant (f-CFT) t-spanner of an n-vertex colored graph G is a subgraph H that preserves distances up to factor t, even in the presence of at most f color faults. This notion generalizes the well-studied f-vertex/edge fault-tolerant (f-V/EFT) spanners. The size (number of edges) of an f-V/EFT spanner crucially depends on the number f of vertex/edge faults to be tolerated. In the colored variants, even a single color fault can correspond to an unbounded number of vertex/edge faults.
The key conceptual contribution of this work is in showing that the size required by an f-CFT spanner is in fact comparable to its uncolored counterpart, with no dependency on the size of color classes. We provide optimal bounds on the size required by f-CFT (2k-1)-spanners, as follows:  
- When vertices have colors, we show an upper bound of O(f^{1-1/k} n^{1+1/k}) edges. This precisely matches the (tight) bounds for (2k-1)-spanners resilient to f individual vertex faults [Bodwin et al., SODA 2018; Bodwin and Patel, PODC 2019].
- For colored edges, we show that O(f n^{1+1/k}) edges are always sufficient. Further, we prove this is tight, i.e., we provide an Ω(f n^{1+1/k}) (worst-case) lower bound. The state-of-the-art bounds known for the corresponding uncolored setting of edge faults are (roughly) Θ(f^{1/2} n^{1+1/k}) [Bodwin et al., SODA 2018; Bodwin, Dinitz and Robelle, SODA 2022].
- We also consider a mixed model where both vertices and edges are colored. In this case, we show tight Θ(f^{2-1/k} n^{1+1/k}) bounds.  Thus, CFT spanners exhibit an interesting phenomenon: while (individual) edge faults are "easier" than vertex faults, edge-color faults are "harder" than vertex-color faults.
Our upper bounds are based on a generalization of the blocking set technique of [Bodwin and Patel, PODC 2019] for analyzing the (exponential-time) greedy algorithm for FT spanners. We complement them by providing efficient constructions of CFT spanners with similar size guarantees, based on the algorithm of [Dinitz and Robelle, PODC 2020].

      Abstract
We initiate the study of spanners in arbitrarily vertex- or edge-colored graphs (with no “legality”
restrictions), that are resilient to failures of entire color classes. When a color fails, all vertices/edges
of that color crash. An f -color fault-tolerant (f -CFT) t-spanner of an n-vertex colored graph G is a
subgraph H that preserves distances up to factor t, even in the presence of at most f color faults.
This notion generalizes the well-studied f -vertex/edge fault-tolerant (f -V/EFT) spanners. The size
(number of edges) of an f -V/EFT spanner crucially depends on the number f of vertex/edge faults
to be tolerated. In the colored variants, even a single color fault can correspond to an unbounded
number of vertex/edge faults.
    The key conceptual contribution of this work is in showing that the size required by an f -CFT
spanner is in fact comparable to its uncolored counterpart, with no dependency on the size of color
classes. We provide optimal bounds on the size required by f -CFT (2k − 1)-spanners, as follows:
    When vertices have colors, we show an upper bound of O(f 1−1/k n1+1/k ) edges. This precisely
    matches the (tight) bounds for (2k − 1)-spanners resilient to f individual vertex faults [Bodwin
    et al., SODA 2018; Bodwin and Patel, PODC 2019].
    For colored edges, we show that O(f n1+1/k ) edges are always sufficient. Further, we prove
    this is tight, i.e., we provide an Ω(f n1+1/k ) (worst-case) lower bound. The state-of-the-art
    bounds known for the corresponding uncolored setting of edge faults are (roughly) Θ(f 1/2 n1+1/k )
    [Bodwin et al., SODA 2018; Bodwin, Dinitz and Robelle, SODA 2022].
   We also consider a mixed model where both vertices and edges are colored. In this case, we show
   tight Θ(f 2−1/k n1+1/k ) bounds.
Thus, CFT spanners exhibit an interesting phenomenon: while (individual) edge faults are “easier”
than vertex faults, edge-color faults are “harder” than vertex-color faults.
   Our upper bounds are based on a generalization of the blocking set technique of [Bodwin and
Patel, PODC 2019] for analyzing the (exponential-time) greedy algorithm for FT spanners. We
complement them by providing efficient constructions of CFT spanners with similar size guarantees,
based on the algorithm of [Dinitz and Robelle, PODC 2020].

88:2   Color Fault-Tolerant Spanners


        1     Introduction
       Let G be an n-vertex weighted graph. A spanner of G is a subgraph that approximately
       preserves distances. Formally, a subgraph H is a t-spanner of G if distH (u, v) ≤ t · distG (u, v)
       for all u, v ∈ V (where distX denotes the shortest path distance in a graph X). Since their
       introduction by Peleg and Ullman [32] and Peleg and Schäffer [30], spanners have been found
       to be extremely useful for a wide variety of applications, including network tasks like routing
       and synchronization [31, 33, 11, 12, 32], distance estimation [34, 2], preconditioning linear
       systems [15], and many others.
           In real-world scenarios, spanners are frequently employed in systems whose components
       are susceptible to occasional breakdowns. It is therefore desirable to have spanners possessing
       resilience to such failures, leading to the notion of fault-tolerant (FT) spanners. Two
       extensively studied types of faults are edge faults and vertex faults. Spanners in the edge/vertex
       fault-tolerant (E/VFT) settings are defined as follows:

       ▶ Definition 1 (E/VFT Spanner). An f -EFT (VFT) t-spanner of G is a subgraph H such
       that for every set F of at most f edges (vertices) in G, it holds that H − F is a t-spanner of
       G − F.

           E/VFT spanners have received major interest in recent years; see, e.g., [8, 13, 4, 7, 14, 5,
       6, 29] and references therein.
           In this work, we introduce and study color fault tolerant models. The framework is
       the following: the edges or vertices are arbitrarily partitioned into classes, or equivalently,
       associated with colors, and f such color classes might fail. Each of the E/VFT settings gets
       a colored counterpart setting, denoted E/VCFT (the C stands for “color”). The standard
       E/VFT settings are obtained as special cases, by giving each edge/vertex a different color.
           Faulty color classes have been used to model Shared Risk Resource Groups (SRRG),
       which arise in many practical contexts such as optical telecommunication networks and multi-
       layered networks; see [10, 23, 35] and references therein for a detailed discussion. Previous
       work in this context mainly focused on colored variants of classical graph problems (and their
       hardness). A notable such problem is diverse routing, where the goal is to determine if two
       (or more) color disjoint paths between two vertices [21, 16, 26] exist (and if so, finding them).
       In such algorithmic contexts, replacing a dense colored graph by a sparse CFT spanner
       could potentially help to improve algorithmic performance, similarly to V/EFT spanners for
       uncolored graphs.

       Sparse Connectivity Certificates. Connectivity certificates are subgraph notions that are
       closely related to FT spanners. Intuitively, a λ-edge (or λ-vertex) connectivity certificate
       serves as concise “proof” to establish the λ-edge/vertex connectivity of a graph G. Formally,
       it is a subgraph H of G such that every two vertices u, v are λ-edge/vertex connected in G if
       and only if they are λ-edge/vertex connected in H. The concept of connectivity certificates
       was presented by Nagamochi and Ibaraki [27], who showed the existence of λ-connectivity
       certificates with at most λ(n − 1) edges for every n-vertex graph. These play a crucial role in
       various graph algorithms [25, 9, 22, 19, 18, 24]. Every λ-V/EFT (2k − 1)-spanner, for every
       1 ≤ k < ∞, is by definition also a λ connectivity certificate, as observed e.g. in [28, 29]. Such
       a spanner with O(λ1−1/k n1+1/k ) edges always exists [7], so choosing k = Θ(log n) yields
       sparse λ-connectivity certificates of O(λn) size.
            Due to the min-cut max-flow theorem, edge/vertex-connectivity can be defined equivalently
       using cuts and flows. In the colored case, this relationship no longer holds: the minimum
       set of colors whose removal disconnects two vertices can be arbitrarily larger than the
A. Petruschka, S. Sapir, and E. Tzalik                                                            88:3


maximum number of color-disjoint paths connecting them [10]. Hence, “color-connectivity
certificates” may take two different meanings for cuts and flows. CFT Spanners can then
be seen as color-connectivity certificates in the cut sense. To avoid confusion, we call the
latter λ-CFT-connectivity certificates. Similarly to their uncolored counterparts, such CFT-
connectivity certificates may provide useful tools when dealing with colored graphs. As this
work focuses on the stronger notion of CFT spanners, (wort-case) optimal results on the size
of CFT-connectivity certificates are implied as direct corollaries.


A Mixed Setting. We additionally consider another possible setting, which we call mixed,
that allows for both edge faults and vertex faults. That is, in the uncolored setting, the
faulty-set F is a subset of V (G) ∪ E(G) of size ≤ f . In the colored setting, both edges
and vertices have colors (and a color may appear on both vertices and edges). We use the
shorthand MFT for the uncolored mixed setting, and MCFT for its colored counterpart. To
the best of our knowledge, MFT spanners have not been explicitly defined, but many known
results for the E/VFT settings implicitly apply to them.


1.1    Our Contribution
We initiate the study of FT spanners supporting f color faults in colored graphs. A naïve
approach for handling color faults is to treat them as many edge/vertex faults. If each color
class contains at most ∆ edges/vertices, then a ∆f -FT spanner for edge/vertex faults is
clearly an f -CFT spanner. While this solution might be plausible for small ∆, it is useless
for large ∆. As the coloring is arbitrary, it may even be that ∆ = Ω(n). Thus, the resulting
spanner from this naïve approach might have Ω(n2 ) edges even when f = 1, i.e., when only
a single color fault may occur. Conceptually, the main contribution of our work is showing
that in the realm of FT spanners, one can handle f color faults almost as efficiently as f
individual edge/vertex faults, without any dependence on ∆.
    Our main results regarding CFT spanners are:

▶ Theorem 2. For every k, f ≥ 1, and every colored n-vertex graph G, there exists an
f -CFT (2k − 1)-spanner with the following size bounds:
1. O(f n1+1/k ) edges in the edge-colored setting,
2. O(f 1−1/k n1+1/k ) edges in the vertex-colored setting, and
3. O(f 2−1/k n1+1/k ) edges in the mixed setting of both edge and vertex colors.
Moreover, the above bounds are tight assuming the Erdős Girth Conjecture.

    Table 1 presents the known bounds for non-colored FT-spanners, compared to the color
settings. The bounds of Theorem 2 are based on the exponential-time FT greedy algorithm.
We further provide polynomial-time constructions of CFT spanners with nearly optimal size
guarantees (up to poly(k) factors). We obtain λ-CFT connectivity certificates as immediate
corollaries:

▶ Theorem 3. Every colored n-vertex graph G has a subgraph H such that, for every two
vertices u, v, and every set C of at most λ colors, u, v are connected in H − C iff they are
connected in G − C, where |E(H)| = O(λn) if the graph has either colored edges or colored
vertices (but not both), and |E(H)| = O(λ2 n) when both vertices and edges are colored. This
is (worst-case) optimal.

       On FT Spanners for Multi-Graphs. Interestingly, the bounds we provide for simple colored
       graphs match the bounds required by E/V/MFT spanners for uncolored multi-graphs. All of
       our results apply both to simple and multi-graphs. This is in contrast to the uncolored setting,
       where “multi” FT-spanners are denser than “simple” ones. See discussion in Appendix A.


       1.2    Technical Overview
       Upper Bounds (Section 3). To prove size upper bounds for CFT spanners, we build upon
       the powerful yet strikingly simple blocking set technique of Bodwin and Patel [7]. This is a
       method for analyzing the spanner H given by the (exponential-time) FT greedy algorithm,
       used in [7] to obtain optimal bounds in the VFT setting. For clarity of exposition, we focus
       our discussion here only on the corresponding vertex-colored setting.
           Bodwin and Patel define a blocking set as a collection of edge-vertex pairs, such that
       each short (≤ 2k) cycle in H contains one of the pairs. On an intuitive level, a graph that
       admits a small blocking set is close to having high girth, forcing it to be sparse. The FT
       greedy algorithm naturally induces a blocking set of size f |E(H)|, which ultimately yields
       the upper bound on the size of H (as explained next). The trivial adaption of this algorithm
       to the CFT settings then leads to the “right” extension of a blocking set: a collection of
       edge-color pairs such that for every short cycle Σ, at least one pair has both its edge and its
       color appearing on Σ.
           The analysis of |E(H)| is by considering a random subgraph of H induced on a fraction
       of ≈ 1/f vertices, and removing the edges of surviving blocking-set-pairs. The resulting
       subgraph, denoted ĤS , has O(n/f ) vertices and large girth, and therefore O((n/f )1+1/k )
       edges according to the folkore Moore Bounds. On the other hand, direct calculations show
       that Ω(|E(H)|/f 2 ) edges are expected to survive, hence |E(H)| = O(f 1−1/k n1+1/k ). Again,
       there seems to be a natural adaptation for (vertex) colors: sample a random fraction of
       ≈ 1/f color classes. The problem that arises is that even though ĤS has O(n/f ) vertices
       in expectation, it is quite probable to have Ω(n) vertices (say, if a color class of size Ω(n) is
       sampled). More conceptually, the problem is that vertices cannot be sampled independently,
       preventing us from using concentration bounds. Naïvely carrying out the same analysis with
       a trivial O(n) bound on the number of sampled vertices yields only an O(f 2 n1+1/k ) bound
       on the size of the spanner H.
A. Petruschka, S. Sapir, and E. Tzalik                                                                 88:5


   We show that even in the independence-deprived circumstances of the VCFT setting,
the same bounds of the VFT setting can be obtained. Our analysis is carefully designed to
harness the little independence we do have, between different color classes. It has three main
ingredients.
(1) We first show that effectively, we may assume that greedy spanner H is color-bipartite:
    a bipartite graph where each color class is fully contained in one of the sides.
(2) To complement this, we use a “symmetric” version of the Moore Bounds: a bipartite
    graph with sides L, R and girth > 2k has O(|L||R|1/k + |R||L|1/k ) edges.1
(3) Combining the independence between the color classes from different sides with the Moore
    Bounds, we show that the random graph ĤS has O((n/f )1+1/k ) edges in expectation.

Lower Bounds (Section 4). Our lower bounds, as most spanner lower bounds, are con-
ditioned on the famous and widely believed Erdős Girth Conjecture [17], implying the
existence of an n-vertex graph GER with Ω(n1+1/k ) edges that has no proper subgraph as a
(2k − 1)-spanner.
    For edge-colored graphs, our strategy is to pack f copies of an n-vertex Erdős graph
GER , denoted G1 , . . . , Gf , on the same set of vertices, with little overlap. We then consider
                 S
the union graph i Gi (ignoring overlaps), where each edge originating from Gi is given the
color i. This graph has Ω(f n1+1/k ) edges, and no proper f -ECFT (2k − 1)-spanner.
    In the mixed-colored setting, we “encode” f 2 disjoint f -ECFT lower bound instances in
a graph with f n properly colored vertices, such that each instance can be isolated by failing
2f vertex-colors. Thus, this graph has no proper 3f -MCFT spanner.

Efficient Algorithms (Section 5). We show efficient CFT spanner constructions based on
the technique of Dinitz and Robelle [14]. Their approach was to modify the greedy algorithm
in the E/VFT settings to have polynomial running time, while ensuring it still induces a small
blocking set, only larger by an O(k) factor than that of the “vanilla” FT greedy algorithm.
Thus, the size analysis based on blocking sets still applies. Our (existential) upper bounds
generalize this last component to colored settings. We then augment the [14] algorithm to
produce small colored blocking sets, and thus achieve efficient constructions.

Remark on Optimality Beyond the Girth Conjecture. Let γ(n, 2k) denote the maximum
number of edges in an n-vertex graph of girth > 2k. The Moore Bounds show that γ(n, 2k) =
O(n1+1/k ), and Erdős’ Girth Conjecture is that this is tight up to a constant factor. Our
lower bounds can be formulated purely in terms of the γ function: Ω(f · γ(n, 2k)) edges in
the ECFT setting, Ω(f 2 · γ(n/f, 2k)) edges in VCFT setting, and Ω(f 3 · γ(n/f, 2k)) edges
in MCFT setting. As for the upper bounds: In the ECFT case, the upper bound matches
the lower bound also in terms of γ. In the VCFT and MCFT settings, the upper bounds
are matching assuming only much weaker conditions on γ than the Girth Conjecture; it
is enough to assume that γ(n, 2k) = Θ(n · β(n, 2k)), where β(·, 2k) is concave (the Girth
Conjecture is that β(n, 2k) = n1/k ).

    2    Preliminaries: A Unified FT Framework
We now present a unified formal framework for all six E/V/M(C)FT settings, to help avoid
tedious repetitions later on.

           Henceforth, assume every edge/vertex x ∈ E(G)∪V (G) is associated with a color c(x) ∈ C,
       where C is some finite set called the color palette. The coloring is arbitrary, and there are
       no “legality” restrictions. For example, two neighboring vertices may share the same color.
       It is also allowed that the same color appears both on edges and on vertices. For c ∈ C,
       we denote the sets of c-colored edges and vertices by Ec (G) = {e ∈ E(G) | c(e) = c} and
       Vc (G) = {v ∈ V (G) | c(v) = c}. The edges of G are weighted, where w(e) = w(u, v) denotes
       the weight of edge e = {u, v}.
           The fault universe F is defined separately for each of the fault-tolerant settings:

       Setting       EFT     VFT          MFT           ECFT           VCFT               MCFT
         F=          E(G)    V (G)    E(G) ∪ V (G)    {Ec (G)}c∈C   {Vc (G)}c∈C    {Ec (G) ∪ Vc (G)}c∈C


           We say that an edge e = {u, v} ∈ E(G) is damaged by x ∈ F if the failure of x causes e
       to fail. Formally, x damages e if: x = e in EFT, x ∈ {u, v} in VFT, x ∈ {e, u, v} in MFT,
       e ∈ x in ECFT, {u, v} ∩ x ̸= ∅ in VCFT, and {e, u, v} ∩ x ≠ ∅ in MCFT. Note that in the
       colored settings, there is a one-to-one correspondence between the fault universe F and the
       set of colors C. So, when S ⊆ F , we say that S contains the color c, and abuse notation by
       writing c ∈ S, when S contains the element corresponding to c from the fault universe F
       (which depends on the setting). We denote by G − S the subgraph of G obtained by deleting
       all edges damaged by some x ∈ S, and by G[S] := G − (F − S), which is the subgraph
       obtained by keeping all edges that can only be damaged by faults from S.
           We now formally state the general FT spanner definition, applying to all settings:

       ▶ Definition 4 (General FT Spanner). An f -FT t-spanner of G with respect to a fault universe
       F (defined by the given setting) is a subgraph H such that for every F ⊆ F with |F | ≤ f , it
       holds that H − F is a t-spanner of G − F .


        3       Upper Bounds
       The FT variant of the greedy spanner algorithm of Alth´’ofer et al. [1], presented as Algorithm 1,
       has been central in the study of spanners in general, and FT spanners in particular.

             Algorithm 1 FTGreedySpanner(G, k, f ).
        1: H ← (V (G), ∅)
        2: for each e = {u, v} ∈ E(G) in increasing order of weight do
        3:    if there is F ⊆ F , |F | ≤ f , not damaging e, such that distH−F (u, v) > (2k − 1)w(e)
           then
        4:        H ← H ∪ {e}
        5: return H


           Aside from its immediate correctness, the greedy approach has been proven to produce
       strong and often optimal upper bounds on the (worst-case) size of E/VFT spanners (e.g.,
       see [7, 6]), making it an “immediate suspect” to investigate for getting upper bounds on the
       size of CFT spanners as well. The major downside of the naïve FT greedy algorithm is its
       exponential-in-f running time, which makes it intractable for many algorithmic applications.
       However, it is often the case that modified polynomial-time greedy approaches (with suitably
       modified analysis) can be devised to produce very close size bounds [5, 14].
A. Petruschka, S. Sapir, and E. Tzalik                                                                         88:7


   In this section, we provide existential size bounds on CFT spanners via the naive FT
greedy algorithm, using the blocking set technique of Bodwin and Patel [7]. We show:

▶ Theorem 5. The number of edges m in the graph H constructed by the FT greedy algorithm
(Algorithm 1) can be bounded as follows:
 1. In the ECFT setting, m = O(f n1+1/k ).
 2. In the VCFT setting, m = O(f 1−1/k n1+1/k ).
 3. In the MCFT setting, m = O(f 2−1/k n1+1/k )


3.1      Blocking Sets and Random Blocked Subgraphs
Denote by H the output of Algorithm 1, and by m its number of edges. The size analysis of
H hinges on a generalized definition of blocking sets, capturing all six E/V/M(C)FT settings.

▶ Definition 6 (Blocking Set). A 2k-blocking set of H is a subset B ⊆ E(H) × F that
sastifies the following conditions:
  (i) If (e, x) ∈ B, then e is not damaged by x.
 (ii) For every cycle Σ in H on ≤ 2k edges, there exist (e, x) ∈ B such that e ∈ Σ, and
       some (other) edge of Σ is damaged by x. Abusing notation, we denote this condition by
      (e, x) ∈ B ∩ Σ.

     The same arguments as in [7] imply the existence of small blocking set for H:

▶ Lemma 7 (Modification of [7, Lemma 3]). There is a 2k-blocking set B of H such that
|B| ≤ f m. Moreover, for every edge e ∈ E(H), there are at most f pairs of the form (e, x)
in B.

Proof. For every e = {u, v} ∈ E(H), let Fe ⊆ F , |Fe | ≤ f be the set of faults not damaging
e that caused e’s insertion. I.e., at the time e was considered by Algorithm 1, it was the case
that distH−Fe (u, v) > (2k − 1)w(e). Define

     B = {(e, x) | e ∈ E(H), x ∈ Fe }.

Every edge e ∈ E(H) participates in at most f pairs (e, x) ∈ B, and condition (i) of
Definition 6 holds. We show condition (ii). Let Σ be a cycle on ≤ 2k edges in H. Consider
the heaviest edge e = {u, v} on Σ.2 Then Σ − e was already present in H before e
was added, forming a u-v path of length ≤ (2k − 1)w(e). But, before adding e, we had
distH−Fe (u, v) > (2k − 1)w(e), so some x ∈ Fe must damage an edge of Σ − e. Thus,
(e, x) ∈ B ∩ Σ.                                                                        ◀

▶ Remark 8. Note that Lemma 7 stays true also for subgraphs of H, by deleting the pairs
from B that correspond to the edges missing in the subgraph.
   To analyze the size of H, we consider the expected number of edges in a randomly-formed
subgraph ĤS of H, which we call a random blocked subgraph. Informally, we bound this
expectation from below by |E(H)|/ poly(f ), and from above by a function of n, f alone.
Rearranging yields the final bounds.

       ▶ Definition 9 (p-Random Blocked Subgraph). Let S ⊆ F be a random subset obtained by
       sampling each x ∈ F into S independently with probably p. Consider H[S], the subgraph of
       H obtained by removing all edges that are damaged by F − S. Essentially, the p-random

       the blocking set. Formally:

 5      Efficient Constructions
We now show an efficient (polynomial time) construction yielding E/V/MCFT spanners
whose sizes match the bounds of Section 3 up to a poly(k) factor:

▶ Theorem 21. There is a polynomial time algorithm for constructing f -CFT (2k − 1)-
spanners, yielding spanner with size s such that:
1. s = O(kf n1+1/k ) in the ECFT setting,
2. s = O(kf 1−1/k n1+1/k ) in the VCFT setting, and
3. s = O(k 2 f 2−1/k n1+1/k ) in the MCFT setting.
The running time is O(mf · s).

    This is by modifying the “Modified FT Greedy Spanner” algorithm of Dinitz and Robelle
[14] to the colored settings. As in [14], we start by considering the case where G is unweighted.
Assume this from now on; we discuss how weights are handled at the end of this section.

The High-Level Idea. Consider the beginning of some iteration of the FT greedy algorithm
(Algorithm 1), which examines e = {u, v} ∈ E(G). The intractable part of the algorithm is
trying to find a fault-set Fe of size ≤ f such that distH−Fe (u, v) > 2k − 1. If no such set is
found, e can clearly be discarded. In the complementary case, e is added to H, and the set
Fe serves to account for ≤ f pairs in the 2k-blocking set constructed by Lemma 7, which
ultimately yields the size bound on the final H.
    Dinitz and Robelle’s idea is replacing this by tractable approximate subroutine, that
settles for finding a set F̃e with size O(kf ), and ensures that e can be discarded if such a set
is not found. This subroutine is based on another greedy approach, of computing a maximal
set of “disjoint” (in some sense) u-v paths of length ≤ 2k − 1 in H. The “blame set” F̃e is
found if the maximal set of paths contains at most f paths, in which case e is inserted to the
spanner. If there are more than f “disjoint” paths, e can be safely discarded. Dinitz and
Robelle [14] consider the VFT setting, where “disjoint” means internally vertex-disjoint, and
the set F̃e contains the internal vertices of those paths. This approach can easily be adapted
to the colored setting, as we now explain.

Subroutine for Deciding on an Edge. The subroutine works in f +1 iterations. We preserve
the invariant that if we completed iteration i without halting, then we have i u-v paths
{Pj }ij=1 in H, each of length ≤ 2k − 1. Furthermore, let Cj be the set of colors appearing

         6      Conclusion
        In this work, we introduced the concept of color fault-tolerant (CFT) spanners, which
        generalize vertex/edge fault-tolerant spanners. We give tight bounds on the size required by
        CFT spanners, and polynomial time constructions of such spanners with nearly optimal size
        guarantees. We suggest a few possible directions for future research:
A. Petruschka, S. Sapir, and E. Tzalik                                                                   88:15


     Can we provide faster algorithms for CFT spanners with size guarantees close to those of
     the FT greedy algorithm? See e.g. the construction by Parter [29] in the VFT setting,
     based on the Baswana-Sen algorithm [3].
     As noted, the min-cut max-flow theorem does not hold in the colored setting. Hence, one
     may consider investigating a different notion from the “color cuts” of CFT-connectivity
     certificates, which pertains to “colorful flow”. That is, a subgraph H of G such that every
     two vertices u, v have λ color-disjoint paths in G iff they have λ such paths in H.

 A     FT Spanners for Multi-Graphs
All of the results in this paper apply also when G is a colored multi-graph, i.e., when many
parallel edges between two vertices are allowed. Especially in edge-colored settings, this
seems like a rather natural assumption in light of the real-world motivation of communication
networks. However, it is presumably less natural in non-colored settings, so explicit discussions
on multi-graphs have mostly been neglected in previous work on FT spanners. We next
provide such a short discussion, which shows an interesting phenomenon: the bounds for
uncolored multi-graphs are the same as for colored simple graphs.

EFT: Θ(f n1+1/k ) size bounds. Our upper bound for ECFT-spanners in Theorem 5(1)
applies for multi-graphs, and EFT is just a special case. Additionally, we note that the
EFT-spanner algorithm of Chechik et al. [8] also works on multi-graphs, and achieves this
size bound. For the lower bound, one may take the Girth Conjecture graph with Ω(n1+1/k )
edges, and give each of its edges multiplicity f . Clearly, such a graph cannot have a proper
f -EFT (2k − 1)-spanner.

VFT: Θ(f 1−1/k n1+1/k ) size bounds. In the VFT setting, parallel edges can be discarded
by keeping the edge of lowest weight among them. This does not change distances (regardless
of which vertex faults occur). Hence, the bounds are the same as for simple graphs.

MFT: Θ(f 2−1/k n1+1/k ) size bounds. Constructing a lower bound instance is easy: Take
the VFT lower bound instance which is a simple graph with Ω(f 1−1/k n1+1/k ) edges and
replace each edge by f parallel edges. Our upper bound for MCFT spanners applies also
here.
